The project team first attempted to develop random mixed-effect negative binomial regressions for the lighting measures but none of the optimization techniques used by SAS could find a global solution for the four models. The researchers therefore developed regular negative binomial regression models, which showed that mean illuminance and illuminance variance were significant, which are listed in Table 28 and Table 29, respectively. As the models suggested, on the major roadways in both cities and after midnight, higher horizontal illuminance levels corresponded with lower nighttime crash frequency. In addition, more uniform lighting (i.e., lower illuminance variance) also correlated with higher nighttime crash frequency. Holding all other variables the same, a 1-lux increase in mean illuminance correlated with a crash modification of 0.983 [i.e., exp(-0.017)], indicating a reduction of 1.7% in nighttime crash frequency. Similarly, a 1-lux increase in illuminance standard deviation corresponded to a 1.8% decrease in crash frequency. Table 28. The analysis involved the following three scenarios: • General nighttime crash analysis. This scenario involved an analysis of all nighttime crashes regardless of dimming periods.
